doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Playing with his wife, singer Nicole Pasternak, and lyrics
summary: He plays differently since marriage, hears lyrics, and describes their record 'In a Word'.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: I thought of this question when you said your wife was a singer. Do you play a melody of a tune differently if it has a well-known lyric?

You know ever since I’ve been married, yes. I mean now I know a lot of the words, I’m not going to lie to you and say I studied the words, even though Lester Young did and a lot of people do. But I’m playing with my wife a lot more, you know, and I hear the lyrics. You know I’m on the bandstand and I listen to her sing, and I say wow that’s a great lyric. And she’s great, and she writes lyrics. And we just did a gig at Cornelia Street in the Village, it was totally jammed. And the reason why they hired her, and they had me too, but they hired her was because she wrote a lot of lyrics on — not the American Songbook — but the jazz. Like “Nica’s Dream,” “Dolphin Dance,” “Sugar” by Stanley Turrentine, and so they wanted her to do it, to hear her lyrics on these songs. And they hired me too because I play. But you know that’s how good she is. So, and then when she sings the song I really hear the lyrics. So it made me appreciate the lyrics more and the song more, definitely. And now hopefully I do, I play differently now that I’m — I can’t recite every lyric but you know I remember the bridge, I remember what it’s trying to say, you know what I mean? You know maybe not specifically all the time like to quote it, like she could, but I’d know what it’s trying to say. You know, it helps. Yeah. Soulful.
What’s it like to, is your wife professional? I mean does she make her living singing?

Oh yeah. Well she’s got a day job too, because no, she’s been a professional for a long time. And we have a couple of records. And we have a record out together, “In a Word,” Don Friedman, Dennis Irwin, Ralph LaLama and Nicole Pasternak, with no drums. And © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

it was totally in a word, now check this out, it’s called “In a Word” and all the titles of the songs are one word: “Smile,” you know, “Four,” “You,” you know I can’t remember everything. But you know it’s like twelve tunes or something, and they’re all one word. So the name of the CD is called “In a Word.”
